# 4,703 people. {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

::: {.section-subtitle}
The opioid overdose epidemic is the worst public health crisis in Pennsylvania, and the nation, in almost a generation. 
:::

## Pennsylvania recorded 4,703 overdose deaths in 2023 {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
import csv
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(open("data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv"))
        if r["year"] == "2023" and r["overdose_deaths"] != ""]
rows = [r for r in rows if r["county"] != "Montour"]

rates = sorted((float(r["rate_per_100k"]), r["county"]) for r in rows)
state = (sum(int(r["overdose_deaths"]) for r in rows)
         / sum(int(r["population"]) for r in rows) * 100000)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.4, 2.6))
ax.scatter([r for r, _ in rates], [0] * len(rates), s=54, color="#003594",
           alpha=0.55, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6, zorder=3)
ax.axvline(state, color="#8a6400", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.6, zorder=2)
ax.text(state + 6, 0.34, f"State rate {state:.1f}", color="#8a6400",
        fontsize=9, ha="center", va="bottom")

for name in ["Forest", "Philadelphia"]:
    value = next(r for r, c in rates if c == name)
    ax.annotate(f"{name} {value:.1f}", (value, 0), xytext=(0, -24),
                textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9, ha="center",
                color="#003594",
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="#6b7280", linewidth=0.8))

ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 0.7)
ax.set_xlim(-3, 92)
ax.set_xlabel("Overdose deaths per 100,000 residents, 2023")
for side in ("left", "right", "top"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#6b7280")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", colors="#6b7280")
ax.text(0.0, -0.58, "Source: PA DOH, Estimated Drug Overdose Deaths, 2023",
        transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=7.5, color="#6b7280")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 1.** Each dot is one Pennsylvania county's overdose death rate in 2023, plotted on
a single axis. The dots spread from Forest County at 0.0 per 100,000 to Philadelphia at
84.8, with most counties clustered between 15 and 40 and the state rate of 36.7 marked by a
dashed line. 
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Today we will discuss....
A state total describes no one. The counties above differ by more than an order of
magnitude, and the state figure conceals that variation entirely.

**This session establishes what that number means for a single county.** The question is
answered at the end, from data, using code we will write together.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Prerequisite assumed
Six weeks of R programming experience, but NOTHING else!
:::



## The data has a named source and a documented limitation {.smaller}

Every dataset in this course traces to a public agency, and every limitation is stated.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Source** | Pennsylvania Department of Health, *Estimated Drug Overdose Deaths* |
| **Coverage** | 67 counties, 2019–2024 |
| **Definition** | Accidental and undetermined drug overdose deaths |
| **Known limitation** | PA DOH marks 2024 **provisional** — death certificates lag three to six months. **This session therefore works in 2023,** the most recent complete year of data available |
| **Second limitation** | Counts of 1–5 are **suppressed**, not published. Seven counties are blank in 2023 |

::: {.callout-important}
## Numbers are reductive! In public health we must remember the human beings behind the numbers.
`4703` is a quantity admitting arithmetic, and will form the basis of several calculations we
do this semester. It is also 4,703 deaths.
:::

# The course. {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

::: {.section-subtitle}
Seven questions to learn about public health in Pennsylvania using Python!
:::

## Seven modules: seven questions about Pennsylvania {.smaller}

Each question is answered with code *that we will write*

::: {.module-map}
|Module | Area | Skill | Question answered |
|:--:|:-------|:---------------|:---------------------|
| **0** | Substance use | Notebook basics and variables | What is Schuylkill County's overdose death rate? |
| **1** | Substance use | Interrogating values, and acting on the answer | Has Centre County met the national overdose target of 13.1 per 100,000? |
| **2** | Infectious disease | Handling many values at once, and code reuse | Which month of the COVID-19 pandemic killed the most Pennsylvanians? |
| **3** | Environmental health | Whole-dataset arithmetic | How far above the EPA fine-particulate standard is the worst county's air? |
| **4** | Newborn health | Reshaping and combining tables to fit a question | Why do some counties not publish an infant mortality rate? |
| **5** | Chronic disease | Constructing figures, and describing what they show | Does adult asthma prevalence move with smoking across all 67 counties? |
| **6** | Injury & violence | Conducting an analysis end to end, reproducibly | Is the rural firearm death rate really lower than the urban one? |
:::

**Every dataset originates with the PA Department of Health, the CDC, or the EPA.**


::: {.callout-important}
## The objective is analytic, not vocational

The purpose of this course is **not** programming proficiency as an end in itself.

The purpose is to pose a question about a population and obtain a defensible answer from
data. **Code is instrumental.**
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Generative AI is not permitted in this course {.smaller}

The prohibition covers labs, homework, and the final project. It is important to have strong
coding skills to understand where AI can produce errors/bugs, verbose code that can be made
more efficient, or even hallucinates.

**This includes inline code completion.** JupyterLab as installed for this course ships no
assistant and requires no action. The prohibition applies to any that is added — a Copilot
extension, an AI-enabled editor opened alongside, or a browser assistant that completes code
in the page.
:::

**Substitutes:** office hours, lab partners, the class channel, the instructor.

::: {.notes}
Give the reason once, without an academic-integrity lecture. Undergraduates respond far
better to "here's why this rule exists" than to a threat, and the reason here is honestly
a good one. Say something like: "I'd rather you submit something broken that you
understand than something perfect that you don't."

The inline-completion point is worth its own sentence because students genuinely do not
classify it as AI use — it feels like autocomplete. The argument that persuades is not the
policy, it is the mechanism: accepting a suggested line removes the moment where you decide
what the code should do, and that moment is the entire skill being taught. Somebody who
accepts six suggestions has a working notebook and has learned nothing, and the course is
six weeks long.

Be candid about the limit of enforcement — it costs nothing and buys credibility: "I cannot
check your laptop. I am not going to try. This works because you decide it works."

If asked about VS Code, some of them will have it from other courses: fine as an editor
provided Copilot is not enabled. Do not let it become a tooling debate; JupyterLab is what
is supported.

The substitutes line matters. Say you mean it, and say when your office hours are.
:::

# Setup. {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

::: {.section-subtitle}
Installing Python on your own machine 
:::

## Six steps, once {.smaller}

The environment is installed locally and takes about fifteen minutes. Steps 1–5 are done
once; step 6 confirms the result.

|Step | Windows | macOS |
|:------|:-------:|:-------:|
| **1.** Open a terminal | PowerShell | Terminal |
|  **2.** Install uv | one line | one line |
| **3.** Download and unzip the course folder | identical | identical |
| **4.** Point the terminal at that folder | identical | identical |
| **5.** Build the environment | `uv sync` | `uv sync` |
| **6.** Check that it worked | `uv run jupyter lab` | `uv run jupyter lab` |

**Python is not downloaded separately. Step 5 installs it.** Anaconda is not required, and
an existing Python or Anaconda installation is left untouched.

::: {.callout-note}
## These instructions are on Canvas
`SETUP.md` carries every step with its failure modes. Nothing here needs to be memorized
or copied down.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide exists so they can see the whole shape before starting, and so nobody spends the
next fifteen minutes wondering how much longer it goes on. Ten seconds on it.

Say the reassuring things now, because half the room is braced for an ordeal. No separate
Python download. No Anaconda. If they already have Python or Anaconda installed, this will
not touch it or fight with it — that is the single most common anxiety and it is worth
pre-empting.

Then set the expectation for the session: everyone does this together, on the projector,
and nobody is behind. This is the one class where setup IS the content.

If somebody is still stuck after ten minutes, pair them with a neighbour and move on. Do
not let one broken laptop consume the session — office hours exist and the syllabus does
not assess installation.
:::

## Step 1 — Open a terminal {.smaller}

A terminal is a window where commands are typed rather than clicked.

| Windows | macOS |
|:--|:--|
| Start button → type `powershell` → open **Windows PowerShell** | `Cmd + Space` → type `terminal` → Return |
| Prompt looks like `PS C:\Users\yourname>` | Prompt looks like `yourname@macbook ~ %` |

Commands are typed at that prompt, exactly as written, each followed by Return.

::: {.notes}
Have the room do this now and physically look up when the window is open. It takes fifteen
seconds and it tells you who is with you before anything can go wrong.

For students who have never opened a terminal — and in this course that is most of them —
name the thing they are feeling: it looks unfriendly and it is not. It is one instruction
at a time, and nothing in this course requires them to be fluent in it.

Worth one sentence: the prompt already tells you which folder you are in. That becomes the
whole point of step 4.
:::

## Step 2 — Install uv {.smaller}

::: {.setup-commands}
<table>
<thead><tr><th>Windows — PowerShell</th><th>macOS — Terminal</th></tr></thead>
<tbody><tr>
<td><code>powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c &quot;irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex&quot;</code></td>
<td><code>curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh</code></td>
</tr></tbody>
</table>
:::

About 35 MB, a few seconds, **no administrator rights and no password**.

::: {.callout-important}
## Then close the terminal and open a new one
The installer changes a setting that only a new window picks up. Confirm with `uv --version`,
which should report a version number.
:::

::: {.notes}
The closing-and-reopening is not a formality and it is the single most common failure in
this entire process. Say it in advance, plainly: "Close the window. Open a new one. This is
not superstition." Otherwise somebody types `uv --version`, sees "not recognized", and
concludes the install failed.

The Windows command must be the full line, including `-ExecutionPolicy ByPass`. The short
version fails on any laptop where script execution is restricted, which describes a lot of
managed machines. Do not let them shorten it.

Ask for hands when `uv --version` prints a number. That is your gate — do not move to step 3
until most of the room has it.
:::

## Step 3 — Download and unzip the course folder {.smaller}

Download `pubhlt0411.zip` from Canvas and **extract it**. Suggested location:

| Windows | macOS |
|:--|:--|
| `C:\Users\yourname\Documents\pubhlt0411` | `/Users/yourname/Documents/pubhlt0411` |

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two failures, both common
**Opening a zip is not extracting it.** Windows displays the contents of a zip without
unpacking them, and Python cannot work inside one. Right-click → *Extract All*.

**Keep the folder out of OneDrive, Dropbox, and Google Drive.** Syncing software interferes
with the files Python creates.
:::

::: {.notes}
The zip trap is a Windows-specific one and it costs somebody twenty minutes every time it
is not pre-empted. Say it as a rule with no exceptions: right-click, Extract All, then work
in the extracted folder.

The OneDrive warning matters more at Pitt than elsewhere, because University accounts push
Documents into OneDrive by default on some configurations. If a student's Documents folder
is synced, have them use the Desktop instead. Worth checking on the projector.
:::

## Step 4 — Point the terminal at that folder {.smaller}

Type `cd` and a space, then **drag the unzipped folder onto the terminal window** and press
Return. Dragging pastes the path correctly, which is faster and more reliable than typing it.

Confirm the location by listing what is there:

| Windows | macOS |
|:--|:--|
| `dir` | `ls` |

**`pyproject.toml` and a `data` folder should appear in the list.** If they do not, the
terminal is pointed somewhere else — repeat this step.

::: {.notes}
The drag-and-drop trick is worth demonstrating rather than describing. It removes the entire
category of typo-in-a-long-path problems, and most students have never seen it.

`cd` means change directory. Say what it does once — it moves the terminal's attention to a
folder — because the concept returns every session and in every FileNotFoundError for the
rest of the course.

The `dir` / `ls` check is the gate again. Make them actually run it and see `pyproject.toml`
before going on. A student who is in the wrong folder at step 4 gets a confusing error at
step 5, and by then the cause is two steps back.
:::

## Step 5 — Build the environment {.smaller}

```bash
uv sync
```

This installs **Python itself** and every package the course uses. A long list of package
names scrolls past; that is expected.

The first run downloads about 200 MB — a minute or two on a good connection, longer on
classroom wifi.

::: {.callout-note}
## Everyone ends up with identical software
`uv sync` reads a lockfile shipped with the course, so every machine in this room installs
the same version of every package. **A result obtained on one laptop is obtainable on any
other** — which is what makes reproducibility something the course can assess.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the step where they wait, so use the time. The lockfile point is the one worth
making out loud, and it connects straight back to the reproducibility criterion on the
assessment slide: "The reason I can hold you to reproducibility is that I have removed the
excuse. You are all running the same thing."

A `.venv` folder appears inside the course folder when this finishes. Tell them what it is
in one sentence — it is their Python installation, it belongs to this course only, and
deleting the course folder removes it completely. That answers the "is this going to clutter
my computer" question before it is asked.

If the download stalls, run it again rather than starting over; uv resumes. On Pitt wifi,
PITTNET beats the guest network by a wide margin.
:::

## Step 6 — Check that it worked {.smaller}

```bash
uv run jupyter lab
```

JupyterLab opens in the browser. In the file list, open **`check_setup.ipynb`** and choose
**Run → Run All Cells**.

::: {.callout-important}
## The notebook prints `SETUP OK`
If it does, the environment is correct and nothing further is required. If it does not, the
message states which check failed.
:::

**To stop JupyterLab:** return to the terminal and press `Ctrl + C` twice.

::: {.notes}
Have everybody run it and say "SETUP OK" out loud, or put a hand up. You want to leave this
room knowing exactly who is working and who is not, because the alternative is discovering
it on Thursday when they are also meeting `if` statements.

The check notebook tests four things: the Python version, that the packages import, that the
data files are findable, and that a real number comes out of a real file. A student who
passes all four is genuinely ready.

Then the daily routine, which is the thing they actually need to retain from this session:
open a terminal, cd into the course folder, `uv run jupyter lab`. Three steps, every time.
Steps 1 through 5 never happen again.
:::

## When something fails {.smaller}

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|:--|:--|
| `uv` is not recognized / command not found | The terminal was not reopened after step 2. Close **all** terminal windows, open a new one. Restart the computer if it persists. |
| Windows: *running scripts is disabled* | The command was shortened. Retype the full line from step 2, including `-ExecutionPolicy ByPass`. |
| macOS: *operation not permitted* | The terminal is denied access to that folder. Move the course folder to `Documents`. |
| `uv sync` stops partway | The network dropped. Run it again — it resumes rather than restarting. |
| `No such file or directory: 'data/...'` | JupyterLab was started outside the course folder. `Ctrl + C`, `cd` to the folder, start again. |

**None of this is assessed.** Unresolved problems go to office hours or
`soumik@pitt.edu` with a screenshot of the terminal.

::: {.notes}
Leave this slide up while you circulate. It is for them to read, not for you to present —
do not narrate the table.

The last line is the one to say out loud, and to mean: nobody in this course falls behind
because of an installation. If they are stuck at the end of the session, they leave with a
plan, not with a problem.

The first row accounts for most of what you will actually see today. Check it first, every
time, before diagnosing anything more interesting.
:::

## A notebook preserves execution state, not screen order {.smaller}

Notebooks contain **code** cells and **text** cells. `Shift+Enter` executes a cell and
advances.

The consequential property: **the interpreter retains what was executed, not what is
displayed.**

```python
population = 143786      # executed first

population = 157795      # executed second

# The first cell is then edited to 999999 and NOT re-executed.
# The value of population remains 157795.
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Execution order is invocation order
Execution does not proceed top to bottom. The bracketed number beside each cell records
the true sequence. This accounts for roughly half of all inexplicable notebook behavior.
:::

**Resolution:** `Kernel > Restart Kernel and Run All Cells`, which is also the test of
whether a notebook is reproducible.

::: {.notes}
This is the most important idea in module 0 and the one with no R-script analogue — a
sourced R script runs top to bottom, always. A notebook does not.

Do the worked example live: run three cells, go back and change the first, don't re-run
it, then print. Ask the room what it will print *before* you press it. Enough people guess
wrong that the point lands hard, and it's much better learned from a wrong guess than from
a slide.

Connect it forward explicitly: "restart and run all" is what reproducibility means in
practice. It is one of the four criteria every submission is marked against, from the first
lab onward, and module 6 is built around it.
:::

## A file is addressed by its path from the course folder {.smaller}

The data files ship with the course, inside a `data` folder. Nothing is uploaded.

```python
pubhlt0411/                        <- start JupyterLab HERE
├── data/
│   └── pa_overdose_county_year.csv
├── check_setup.ipynb
└── pyproject.toml
```

A file is then read by its **relative path** — its location starting from the course folder:

```python
pd.read_csv("data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The path is relative to where JupyterLab was started
`FileNotFoundError` on a file that plainly exists almost always means JupyterLab was
started somewhere other than the course folder. **Stop it, `cd` to the course folder,
start it again.**
:::

::: {.notes}
This replaces a whole category of Colab misery — no uploading, no re-uploading the same CSV
four times in one lab, no Drive permissions pop-up. The files are simply there.

The one failure mode worth drilling is the relative path, and it is worth demonstrating
rather than describing. Start JupyterLab from the wrong folder deliberately, run the read,
and show them the FileNotFoundError. Then fix it in front of them. A student who has seen
that error once diagnoses it in ten seconds; a student who has not will email you.

Say the rule as a habit rather than a fact: "Always start Jupyter from the course folder.
When a file is missing, that is the first thing to check, before you check the spelling."

Relative paths also matter for a reason beyond convenience, and it is worth one sentence:
`data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv` works on every machine in this room. A path like
`C:\Users\yourname\Desktop\stuff.csv` works on exactly one. That is the difference between
an analysis someone else can run and one they cannot.
:::

# Values. {.unnumbered background-color="#003594"}

::: {.section-subtitle}
"The time has come," the Walrus said, "to talk of many things".

-- Lewis Carroll, Through the Looking-Glass.
:::

## Assignment binds a name to a value {.smaller}

The `=` operator does not assert equality. It **binds**: the expression on the right is
evaluated, and the name on the left refers to the result.

```{pyodide}
county = "Schuylkill"
overdose_deaths = 60
population = 143786

print(county)
print(overdose_deaths)
```

The statement is read right to left: construct the value, then attach the name.

::: {.callout-tip}
## R analogue
`county <- "Schuylkill"`. The semantics are equivalent. Python uses `=` and provides no
`<-`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Say the right-to-left reading out loud — it's worth thirty seconds. Students who read `=`
as "equals" get stuck in module 2 on `count = count + 1`, which is nonsense as an equation
and obvious as an instruction.

These are the real 2023 Schuylkill County numbers, and they stay these numbers all
semester. When Schuylkill comes back in module 1, it comes back with the same variable
names and the same values. That consistency is deliberate — tell them the stories recur.
:::

## Identifier choice is a documentation decision {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
# Syntactically valid, semantically opaque.
x = 60
y = 143786

# Syntactically valid, self-documenting.
overdose_deaths = 60
population = 143786

print(overdose_deaths / population * 100000)
```

**Constraints:** letters, digits, underscores; no spaces; no leading digit. Identifiers are
case-sensitive — `Population` and `population` denote different names.

**Convention:** `lower_case_with_underscores`, not `PopulationCount`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Readability is an assessed criterion
Identifier quality falls under presentation, which is a named grading criterion in this
course.
:::

::: {.notes}
Don't soften this one. The habit forms in the first week or it doesn't form at all, and
the cost of `x` stays invisible until the notebook is long enough to hurt. Tell them: "`x`
costs you marks here, and it costs your future self twenty minutes."

R conventions are often `dot.separated` or `camelCase`. Python is near-universally
`snake_case`. One line, then move on.
:::

## Every value carries a type that determines valid operations {.smaller}

Four types account for nearly all data handled in this course.

```{pyodide}
county = "Schuylkill"        # str   — text
overdose_deaths = 60         # int   — whole number
rate_per_100k = 41.7         # float — decimal number
is_rural = True              # bool  — True or False

print(type(county))
print(type(overdose_deaths))
print(type(rate_per_100k))
print(type(is_rural))
```

`type()` reports the type of any value and is the appropriate diagnostic when an operation
behaves unexpectedly.

::: {.callout-tip}
## R analogue
`character`, `integer`, `numeric`, `logical`. Python writes `True` and `False`, not `TRUE`
and `FALSE`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Stress the capital `T`. `TRUE` raises a NameError in Python and it's the single most common
import from R muscle memory — they will all do it at least once.

Worked example: ask what `type(60)` and `type(60.0)` return. Same number to a human, `int`
and `float` to Python. That distinction is exactly what produces the division surprise two
slides from now, so plant it here.
:::

## Exercise: bind one county's values {.smaller}

Centre County, 2023: seven deaths, population 157,795.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: m0_assign
county = "Centre"
overdose_deaths = ______
population = 157795

print(county, overdose_deaths, population)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: m0_assign
#| hint: true
# Seven deaths, written as a whole number without quotation marks.
# Quoted, the value becomes the string "7", which does not support division.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: m0_assign
#| solution: true
county = "Centre"
overdose_deaths = 7
population = 157795

print(county, overdose_deaths, population)
```

::: {.notes}
Fill this in with the room rather than letting them work alone. It's the first `{pyodide}`
cell they touch, and the point is the mechanics of running a cell, not the difficulty of
the blank.

Before you type the answer, ask why `"7"` in quotes would be wrong. Somebody will say "it's
text" — promise them the TypeError slide is two slides away and that they're about to see
exactly what goes wrong.

Centre County is the counterweight to Schuylkill and returns in module 1 as the direct
comparison.
:::

## Python does not coerce between text and numbers {.smaller}

**Scenario:** a file supplies `"60"` as text. Adding eight should yield `68`.

```{pyodide}
overdose_deaths = "60"

try:
    print(overdose_deaths + 8)
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `TypeError` — unsupported operand types
`TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str`

The `+` operator is defined for `str + str` (concatenation) and for `int + int` (addition),
but not across the two. Rather than infer an intent, the interpreter raises.

**Resolution:** convert explicitly — `int(overdose_deaths) + 8`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Run it broken and read the printed line out loud. Two parts, and both matter: the error's
NAME on the left of the colon, and the explanation on the right. Students who learn to read
the name first diagnose faster, because the name is what they can search for.

The `try`/`except` wrapper is scaffolding, not syntax they need today — say so in one
sentence if anyone asks, and tell them it is how a program handles an error instead of
stopping. Do not teach it; module 6 does.

Then fix it live and re-run: delete the wrapper, write `int(overdose_deaths) + 8`, and show
the 68.

Be candid: everybody hits this one, including you, all semester. Data read from a file
arrives as text constantly. Tell them they'll stop being surprised by it around week three.

Point out that this error is loud, and that loud is a gift — the dangerous errors are the
silent ones that hand you a wrong number without complaint. That's the next slide.
:::

## Conversion between types is explicit {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
deaths_as_text = "60"

print(int(deaths_as_text) + 8)        # 68  — numeric addition
print(deaths_as_text + "8")           # 608 — string concatenation
print(float("41.7"))                  # text to floating point
print(str(60) + " deaths")            # numeric to text
print(int(41.7))                      # 41  — truncation, not rounding
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `int()` truncates toward zero
`int(41.7)` evaluates to `41`. The fractional component is discarded rather than rounded.
`round(41.7)` performs rounding and evaluates to `42`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Pause on the `608` line. It is not an error — Python did exactly what it was told and
produced a wrong answer in silence. That's the more dangerous failure mode and this is the
first time they see it. Ask them how they'd catch it. The answer is `type()`, and that they
have to be suspicious.

Truncation bites whenever they compute a per-something count. If you want a second example,
show `int(70.2)` returning 70 — that's the average deaths per county, and losing 0.2 of a
person is a real distortion.
:::

## Seven arithmetic operators {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
print(4703 + 67)      # addition
print(4703 - 67)      # subtraction
print(4703 * 2)       # multiplication
print(4703 / 67)      # division       -> float, always
print(4703 // 67)     # floor division -> 70, remainder discarded
print(4703 % 67)      # modulo         -> 13, the remainder
print(2 ** 10)        # exponentiation -> 1024
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Three operators warrant particular attention
`/` returns a `float` even when the division is exact. `//` discards the remainder.
Exponentiation is `**`; the `^` operator denotes bitwise exclusive-or and **evaluates
without error to an incorrect result** when used for powers.
:::

::: {.notes}
`^` is the R import that hurts most. In R, `2^10` is 1024. In Python, `2^10` is 8 — wrong,
silent, and plausible-looking enough to survive a code review. Demonstrate it if there's
time; the silence is the whole lesson.

`%` corresponds to R's `%%`. One character, same job. Mention it and move on.
:::

## Exercise: compute a rate per 100,000 {.smaller}

A rate per 100,000 is the count divided by the population, multiplied by 100,000.
Schuylkill County, 2023.

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: m0_rate
overdose_deaths = 60
population = 143786

rate_per_100k = overdose_deaths / population * ______

print(rate_per_100k)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: m0_rate
#| hint: true
# The multiplier is 100000, written without a comma separator.
# Python parses 100,000 as two values, not one, and the result will not be a rate.
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: m0_rate
#| solution: true
overdose_deaths = 60
population = 143786

rate_per_100k = overdose_deaths / population * 100000

print(rate_per_100k)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The output carries excessive precision
`41.728680121847745` is arithmetically correct and unsuitable for presentation. Formatting
is addressed on the following slide.
:::

::: {.notes}
The comma warning in the hint is not hypothetical. `100,000` is legal Python that means
something completely different — it builds a tuple — so it fails confusingly rather than
cleanly. Somebody will do it.

They have computed a rate in R already. Say so: this is the same arithmetic they already
know, and the only new thing is where Python wants the parentheses.

Leave the ugly output on screen. Don't clean it up — it's the motivation for the next
slide, and they should feel the need before they're handed the tool.
:::

## f-strings interpolate values into text {.smaller}

An `f` prefix on a string literal causes each `{expression}` to be evaluated and
substituted.

```{pyodide}
county = "Schuylkill"
rate_per_100k = 41.72

print(f"{county} County: {rate_per_100k} per 100,000")
print(f"{county} County: {rate_per_100k:.1f} per 100,000")
```

The `:.1f` format specifier fixes the output at one digit after the decimal point; `:.2f`
gives two.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Format at presentation, retain full precision in computation
Rounding applied at the point of printing does not affect stored values. Rounding applied
during computation propagates through every subsequent step.
:::

::: {.notes}
`.1f` is the one they'll use constantly. This course reports rates to one decimal by
convention, because a second decimal implies a precision the underlying data doesn't
support — worth saying, since they'll otherwise copy whatever Python prints.

R analogue: `sprintf("%.1f", x)` or `glue()`. One line.

The forward-looking point is real, not theoretical. In module 4 they compute group rates
across many counties, and rounding at the wrong step there produces totals that are
visibly, embarrassingly wrong.
:::

## Comments document rationale, not syntax {.smaller}

Text following `#` is ignored by the interpreter and addressed to the reader.

```{pyodide}
# Redundant: restates the operation.
rate_per_100k = 60 / 143786 * 100000   # divide deaths by population

# Substantive: records a decision about the data.
# PA DOH suppresses counts of 1-5. Counties below that threshold are
# blank rather than zero; a blank does not indicate the absence of deaths.
overdose_deaths = 60

print(f"{rate_per_100k:.1f}")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Comments are assessed
Interpretation and presentation together account for the majority of the grading criteria.
Comments are where analytic reasoning becomes visible to a reader.
:::

::: {.notes}
The suppression comment is a genuine preview of module 4, where blank-versus-zero becomes
an entire teaching case. Forest County has both, in the same column, in the real file —
mention that if you want to make it concrete.

The rule to give them out loud: comment the decision, not the syntax. If a line's *what*
isn't obvious, the fix is usually a better variable name rather than a comment explaining
a bad one.
:::

Answering the question this session opened with

## The source file is accessible from this session {.smaller}

`data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv` — 402 observations across 67 counties, 2019–2024.

```{pyodide}
with open("data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv") as handle:
    for line in handle:
        print(line.rstrip())
        break
```

The first line is the header, naming each column.

```{pyodide}
with open("data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv") as handle:
    lines = handle.readlines()

print(f"Rows in the file: {len(lines)}")
print(lines[1].rstrip())
print(lines[2].rstrip())
```

::: {.notes}
Do not teach file reading here. This is a demonstration that the file is real and
reachable — they watch it, they don't reproduce it. Module 2 teaches loops and module 4
teaches pandas; both open this same file properly.

What to point at: the header names, and that 403 lines is 402 county-years plus one header
row. Real files have a header, and forgetting it is a classic off-by-one that will bite
them in module 2.
:::

## Two counties of comparable population {.smaller}

Schuylkill and Centre, 2023. Both approximately 150,000 residents.

```{pyodide}
schuylkill_deaths = 60
schuylkill_population = 143786

centre_deaths = 7
centre_population = 157795

schuylkill_rate = schuylkill_deaths / schuylkill_population * 100000
centre_rate = centre_deaths / centre_population * 100000

print(f"Schuylkill: {schuylkill_rate:.1f} per 100,000")
print(f"Centre:     {centre_rate:.1f} per 100,000")
print(f"Ratio:      {schuylkill_rate / centre_rate:.1f}x")
```

::: {.notes}
Run it, then stop talking. Let the output do the work — resist narrating over the moment
the ratio appears.

These are the real 2023 rows from the file on the previous slide: 60 deaths in Schuylkill,
7 in Centre. Centre's low count is partly a young student population, which is module 1's
argument and not today's.

If a student asks "why is it so different?", the honest answer is "that's Thursday's entire
lecture." Say it that way — the question is the hook for module 1, and answering it now
spends it.
:::

## The state figure resolves into a ninefold difference {.smaller}

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
import csv
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(open("data/pa_overdose_county_year.csv"))
        if r["year"] == "2023" and r["overdose_deaths"] != ""]
rows = [r for r in rows if r["county"] != "Montour"]

rates = sorted((float(r["rate_per_100k"]), r["county"]) for r in rows)
state = (sum(int(r["overdose_deaths"]) for r in rows)
         / sum(int(r["population"]) for r in rows) * 100000)

highlight = {"Centre": "#8a6400", "Schuylkill": "#003594"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.4, 2.6))

# Every other county recedes into the background.
ax.scatter([r for r, c in rates if c not in highlight],
           [0] * (len(rates) - len(highlight)),
           s=54, color="#6b7280", alpha=0.30,
           edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6, zorder=3)

# The two counties of the comparison, marked by colour AND shape AND label.
for name, colour in highlight.items():
    value = next(r for r, c in rates if c == name)
    marker = "D" if name == "Schuylkill" else "s"
    ax.scatter([value], [0], s=150, color=colour, marker=marker,
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.4, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(f"{name}\n{value:.1f}", (value, 0), xytext=(0, -30),
                textcoords="offset points", fontsize=10, ha="center",
                color=colour, fontweight="bold",
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=colour, linewidth=1.0))

ax.axvline(state, color="#6b7280", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, zorder=2)
# Label sits LEFT of the line and BELOW the span arrow: the Schuylkill marker is
# at 41.7 and the arrow runs across y=0.62, so the slide-3 placement would
# collide with both.
ax.text(state - 1.5, 0.14, f"State rate {state:.1f}", color="#6b7280",
        fontsize=9, ha="right", va="bottom")

ax.annotate("", xy=(41.7, 0.62), xytext=(4.4, 0.62),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="#003594", linewidth=1.3))
ax.text(23.0, 0.68, "9.5x", color="#003594", fontsize=11,
        fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="bottom")

ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_ylim(-0.9, 1.05)
ax.set_xlim(-3, 92)
ax.set_xlabel("Overdose deaths per 100,000 residents, 2023")
for side in ("left", "right", "top"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#6b7280")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", colors="#6b7280")
ax.text(0.0, -0.62, "Source: PA DOH, Estimated Drug Overdose Deaths, 2023",
        transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=7.5, color="#6b7280")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.figure-description}
**Figure 2.** The same 59 Pennsylvania counties shown at the start of this session, with two
marked. Centre County, a gold square at 4.4 deaths per 100,000, sits near the low end of the
distribution; Schuylkill County, a blue diamond at 41.7, sits in the upper third. An arrow
spans the two, labelled 9.5x. The state rate of 36.7 is marked by a dashed line. Every other
county is greyed.
:::

**Comparable populations. A ninefold difference in rate.**

::: {.callout-important}
## What the state total concealed
4,703 describes Pennsylvania. It resolves into 41.7 in one county and 4.4 in another, and
no resident experiences the state average.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the payoff. Land it and stop — do not add another point after it.

The figure is deliberately the same one that opened the session, and the callback is the
whole point. Say so: "This is the picture I showed you an hour ago. Nothing about it has
changed. The only difference is that you can now find yourself on it."

Give them a beat to locate the two marked counties among the grey ones. The visual argument
is that these are not freak values at the extreme ends — Centre is near the bottom but
Schuylkill is not the top, it is an ordinary county in the upper third. The gap between two
unremarkable counties is ninefold. That is a stronger claim than min-versus-max, and it is
worth making out loud because the eye does not make it automatically.

Then the closing line, plainly: "Two counties, nearly the same size. There's the gap. You
wrote the code that found it, in your first hour of Python." That sentence is spoken, not
printed — it's the promise from the cold open being paid off, and it works because they did
the work.

Then hold the door open for Thursday: which county is which, and how would you know without
me telling you? Module 1 makes them classify it themselves.
:::

## Session outcomes {.smaller}

- Installing the course environment, and verifying it with `check_setup.ipynb`
- Executing cells in JupyterLab, and accounting for **execution order as invocation order**
- Reading a data file by its path relative to the course folder
- Binding values to descriptive identifiers
- Distinguishing `int`, `float`, `str`, and `bool` via `type()`, and converting between them
- Applying arithmetic operators, including `//`, `%`, and `**`
- Formatting output with f-strings and the `:.1f` specifier
